papers.abstract: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? In this work, we provide evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating -- a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. We integrate the model-agnostic theory of optimal prediction with mechanistic interpretability to analyze transformers trained on a tractable family of hidden Markov models that generate rich geometric patterns in neural activations. Our primary analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, revealing how the first attention layer implements these constrained updates, with extensions to multi-layer architectures demonstrating how subsequent layers refine these representations. We find that attention carries out an algorithm with a natural interpretation in the probability simplex, and create representations with distinctive geometric structure. We show how both the algorithmic behavior and the underlying geometry of these representations can be theoretically predicted in detail -- including the attention pattern, OV-vectors, and embedding vectors -- by modifying the equations for optimal future token predictions to account for the architectural constraints of attention. Our approach provides a principled lens on how architectural constraints shape the implementation of optimal prediction, revealing why transformers develop specific intermediate geometric structures.

papers.title: Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals
papers.research_question: How do different mechanisms interact in the decision-making of LLMs? The paper proposes to trace how one mechanism becomes dominant in the final prediction.
papers.core_contribution: The paper formulates the competition of mechanisms and traces how mechanisms compete within LLMs, identifying critical components and attention positions that control the strength of mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates how to trace the competition of mechanisms in LLMs and reveals insights into how factual and counterfactual mechanisms interact and can be controlled.
papers.key_findings:
In early layers, the factual attribute is encoded in the subject position, while the counterfactual is in the attribute position.
The attention blocks write most of the factual and counterfactual information to the last position.
All the highly activated heads attend to the attribute position regardless of the specific type of information they promote. The factual information flows by penalizing the counterfactual attribute rather than promoting the factual one.
We can up-weight the value of a few very localized values of the attention head matrix to strengthen factual mechanisms substantially.
Similar tokens confuse the model more easily, and larger models suffer more from such confusion.
papers.limitation: Logit inspection can occasionally fail to reflect the actual importance of vocabulary items, especially in the early layers of the network.
future_direction: Extend the competition of mechanisms formulation to more complex mechanisms and multi-step reasoning.
Explore other mechanisms and their competitions in future work.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research aims to bridge the gap between empirical success and our scientific understanding of the inner workings of large language models (LLMs). However, most existing research focuses on analyzing a single mechanism, such as how models copy or recall factual knowledge. In this work, we propose a formulation of competition of mechanisms, which focuses on the interplay of multiple mechanisms instead of individual mechanisms and traces how one of them becomes dominant in the final prediction. We uncover how and where mechanisms compete within LLMs using two interpretability methods: logit inspection and attention modification. Our findings show traces of the mechanisms and their competition across various model components and reveal attention positions that effectively control the strength of certain mechanisms. Code: https://github.com/francescortu/comp-mech. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/francescortu/comp-mech.

papers.title: On the Generalizability of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals"
papers.research_question: Does the competition of mechanisms between factual recall and counterfactual repetition, as identified by Ortu et al. (2024), generalize to larger models, different prompt structures, and across domains?
papers.core_contribution: The attention head ablation method from Ortu et al. (2024) does not generalize well; its effectiveness varies significantly with model architecture, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.conclusion: The competition of mechanisms identified by Ortu et al. (2024) is not fully generalizable; experimental findings in mechanistic interpretability are highly dependent on the specific model, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully reproduced the original findings on GPT-2 small and Pythia 6.9B regarding positional information encoding, attention block dominance, and attention head specialization.
In Llama 3.1 8B, attention head specialization is greatly reduced, and the logit lens method shows limited early-layer activity and a sharp final-layer activation.
Changing the prompt structure to a question-answering format reduces the model's propensity to repeat the counterfactual, indicating sensitivity to repetition.
The choice of premise word (e.g., 'Redefine', 'Validate') affects the rate of factual vs. counterfactual predictions and the effectiveness of attention head ablation.
The effectiveness of the proposed attention head ablation varies across domains; it works best for domains where the factual token is leaked in the subject (e.g., 'Autos and Vehicles') and fails for others.
papers.limitation:
The logit lens method may be unreliable for larger models like Llama 3.1 8B, potentially failing to capture early-layer mechanisms.
The filtered MQuAKE dataset used for domain analysis is very small (228 prompts), limiting definitive conclusions.
Most extended findings rely on GPT-2 small and a dataset derived from Ortu et al. (2024), limiting generalizability to other models and datasets.
future_direction: Investigate whether larger models distribute work more evenly across heads or if newer interpretability techniques (e.g., circuit analysis, tuned lens) are needed to capture their mechanisms.
Conduct a deeper analysis of why certain dataset domains impact attention head activation, distinguishing between token leakage, topic words, and task difficulty.
Extend the findings to different, larger datasets and models, as well as new prompt structures and premise words.
papers.abstract: We present a reproduction study of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals" (Ortu et al., 2024), which investigates competition of mechanisms in language models between factual recall and counterfactual in-context repetition. Our study successfully reproduces their primary findings regarding the localization of factual and counterfactual information, the dominance of attention blocks in mechanism competition, and the specialization of attention heads in handling competing information. We reproduce their results on both GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and Pythia 6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023). We extend their work in three significant directions. First, we explore the generalizability of these findings to even larger models by replicating the experiments on Llama 3.1 8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), discovering greatly reduced attention head specialization. Second, we investigate the impact of prompt structure by introducing variations where we avoid repeating the counterfactual statement verbatim or we change the premise word, observing a marked decrease in the logit for the counterfactual token. Finally, we test the validity of the authors' claims for prompts of specific domains, discovering that certain categories of prompts skew the results by providing the factual prediction token as part of the subject of the sentence. Overall, we find that the attention head ablation proposed in Ortu et al. (2024) is ineffective for domains that are underrepresented in their dataset, and that the effectiveness varies based on model architecture, prompt structure, domain and task.

papers.title: Reducing Bias in Sentiment Analysis Models Through Causal Mediation Analysis and Targeted Counterfactual Training
papers.research_question: How to reduce bias in sentiment analysis models by leveraging causal mediation analysis to identify biased components and applying targeted counterfactual training for de-biasing.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a bias reduction method for sentiment analysis models that uses causal mediation analysis to identify layers causally implicated in gender bias and then applies counterfactual training only to those targeted layers, achieving improved fairness without loss of accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method successfully reduces gender bias in BERT sentiment models by using causal mediation analysis to target specific layers and then applying counterfactual training, resulting in improved fairness without compromising accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Causal mediation analysis can identify specific layers in BERT that contribute to gender bias.
Targeted counterfactual training on those identified layers reduces bias effectively.
The proposed method achieves higher fairness (lower Wasserstein distance) compared to baseline methods like full-model counterfactual training and dropout regularization.
The method maintains sentiment prediction accuracy while improving fairness, avoiding the accuracy-fairness trade-off.
The approach is validated on two sentiment analysis datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and evaluated on the Equity Evaluation Corpus (EEC).
papers.limitation: Limited to two datasets (SST-2 and Amazon reviews) and one fairness metric (p-Wasserstein).
future_direction: Apply the method to other biases on sensitive attributes such as ethnic groups, skin colour, and country.
Test the method on a broader range of datasets and with more fairness evaluation techniques.
Quantify the accuracy-fairness trade-off in real-world datasets.
papers.abstract: Large language models provide high-accuracy solutions in many natural language processing tasks. In particular, they are used as word embeddings in sentiment analysis models. However, these models pick up on and amplify biases and social stereotypes in the data. Causality theory has recently driven the development of effective algorithms to evaluate and mitigate these biases. Causal mediation was used to detect biases, while counterfactual training was proposed to mitigate bias. In both cases, counterfactual sentences are created by changing an attribute, such as the gender of a noun, for which no change in the model output is expected. Biases are detected and eventually corrected each time the model behaviour differs between the original and the counterfactual sentence. We propose a new method for de-biasing sentiment analysis models that leverages the causal mediation analysis to identify the parts of the model primarily responsible for the bias and apply targeted counterfactual training for model de-biasing. We validated the methodology by fine-tuning the pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model for sentiment prediction. We trained two sentiment analysis models using the Stanford Sentiment Treebank dataset and the Amazon Product Reviews, respectively, and we evaluated the fairness and prediction performances using the Equity Evaluation Corpus. We illustrated the causal patterns in the network and showed that our method achieves both high fairness and more accurate sentiment analysis than the state-of-the-art approach. Contrary to state-of-the-art models, we achieved a noticeable improvement in gender fairness without hindering sentiment prediction accuracy.

papers.title: CaKE: Circuit-aware Editing Enables Generalizable Knowledge Learners
papers.research_question: Why do current knowledge editing methods fail to generalize updated knowledge to multi-hop reasoning tasks, and how can this be improved?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CaKE, a circuit-aware knowledge editing method that improves the integration of updated knowledge into reasoning circuits, enabling better generalization in multi-hop reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: CaKE aligns knowledge editing with the inherent reasoning architectures of LLMs, enabling generalizable multi-hop knowledge editing.
papers.key_findings:
Current knowledge editing methods like ROME and WISE fail in multi-hop reasoning due to misalignment with reasoning circuits.
CaKE outperforms existing methods on multi-hop benchmarks, achieving an average improvement of 20% in accuracy.
CaKE requires only a few curated data samples to integrate knowledge effectively.
CaKE maintains model locality and general ability while editing knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on factual knowledge and multi-hop reasoning, not other domains like math or long-form reasoning.
Does not deeply investigate fine-grained circuit components like relational information.
Connection between model abilities and training data is underexplored.
future_direction: Investigate knowledge editing in other reasoning domains such as long-form mathematics.
Explore enhancement of knowledge utilization in slow-thinking paradigms like chain-of-thought.
Develop more concise methods for knowledge editing focusing on fine-grained circuit components.
papers.abstract: Knowledge Editing (KE) enables the modification of outdated or incorrect information in large language models (LLMs). While existing KE methods can update isolated facts, they often fail to generalize these updates to multi-hop reasoning tasks that rely on the modified knowledge. Through an analysis of reasoning circuits -- the neural pathways LLMs use for knowledge-based inference, we find that current layer-localized KE approaches (e.g., MEMIT, WISE), which edit only single or a few model layers, inadequately integrate updated knowledge into these reasoning pathways. To address this limitation, we present CaKE (Circuit-aware Knowledge Editing), a novel method that enhances the effective integration of updated knowledge in LLMs. By only leveraging a few curated data samples guided by our circuit-based analysis, CaKE stimulates the model to develop appropriate reasoning circuits for newly incorporated knowledge. Experiments show that CaKE enables more accurate and consistent use of edited knowledge across related reasoning tasks, achieving an average improvement of 20% in multi-hop reasoning accuracy on the MQuAKE dataset while requiring less memory than existing KE methods. We release the code and data in https://github.com/zjunlp/CaKE.

papers.title: Patchscopes: A Unifying Framework for Inspecting Hidden Representations of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we leverage the model itself to explain its internal representations in natural language, and how can a configurable patching framework be used to decode information from hidden representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Patchscopes, a modular framework for decoding information from hidden representations in LLMs, which unifies prior interpretability methods and enables more expressive, robust, and training-data-free inspection.
papers.conclusion: Patchscopes provides a unifying framework for inspecting hidden representations that mitigates shortcomings of prior methods and opens up new possibilities for more expressive and robust interpretation, including practical benefits like correcting multi-hop reasoning errors.
papers.key_findings:
Patchscopes outperforms vocabulary projection methods (Logit Lens, Tuned Lens) in decoding next-token predictions from intermediate layers across multiple models.
Patchscopes can extract specific attributes from hidden representations without training data, outperforming linear probes in 6 out of 12 commonsense and factual reasoning tasks.
Patchscopes can verbalize the gradual entity resolution process in early layers, where vocabulary projections fail.
Patchscopes enables cross-model inspection, allowing a more capable model to explain representations of a smaller model.
Patchscopes can correct latent multi-hop reasoning errors, achieving 50% accuracy on a complex task, outperforming chain-of-thought and vanilla generation.
papers.limitation:
The framework only reveals if specific information can be decoded from the patched representation via the post-patching computation, but does not guarantee the representation stores all that information.
The method may suffer from placeholder contamination where the placeholder token in the target prompt interferes with the generation.
future_direction: Quantify qualitative observations of entity resolution and placeholder contamination.
Study to what extent placeholder contamination can be mitigated with a different placeholder choice.
Investigate why some models might be more susceptible to placeholder contamination than others.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) can help explain models' behavior and verify their alignment with human values. Given the capabilities of LLMs in generating human-understandable text, we propose leveraging the model itself to explain its internal representations in natural language. We introduce a framework called Patchscopes and show how it can be used to answer a wide range of questions about an LLM's computation. We show that many prior interpretability methods based on projecting representations into the vocabulary space and intervening on the LLM computation can be viewed as instances of this framework. Moreover, several of their shortcomings such as failure in inspecting early layers or lack of expressivity can be mitigated by Patchscopes. Beyond unifying prior inspection techniques, Patchscopes also opens up new possibilities such as using a more capable model to explain the representations of a smaller model, and multihop reasoning error correction.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: When Only Time Will Tell: Interpreting How Transformers Process Local Ambiguities Through the Lens of Restart-Incrementality
papers.research_question: How do restart-incremental Transformers build and update internal states when processing local ambiguities, and what processes cause revisions not viable in autoregressive models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an interpretable method to analyze the internal states of restart-incremental Transformers, showing that their sequential structure encodes information on garden path effects and resolution, and that bidirectional models update states to resolve ambiguities.
papers.conclusion: Restart-incremental models can revise internal states when processing local ambiguities, and the proposed method provides insights into how these revisions occur, highlighting the advantage of bidirectional models over causal ones for revision.
papers.key_findings:
Future tokens affect the meaning representation of previous tokens in bidirectional models, with larger effects when there is a linguistic motivation to revise (e.g., in garden path sentences).
In bidirectional models, states are updated to absorb new interpretations when disambiguating tokens are integrated, aligning with output revisions.
Causal models (like GPT-2) encode differences in intermediate layers between ambiguous and unambiguous sentences, but their final layer states are similar, indicating they do not revise.
papers.abstract: Incremental models that process sentences one token at a time will sometimes encounter points where more than one interpretation is possible. Causal models are forced to output one interpretation and continue, whereas models that can revise may edit their previous output as the ambiguity is resolved. In this work, we look at how restart-incremental Transformers build and update internal states, in an effort to shed light on what processes cause revisions not viable in autoregressive models. We propose an interpretable way to analyse the incremental states, showing that their sequential structure encodes information on the garden path effect and its resolution. Our method brings insights on various bidirectional encoders for contextualised meaning representation and dependency parsing, contributing to show their advantage over causal models when it comes to revisions.

papers.title: Know More, Know Clearer: A Meta-Cognitive Framework for Knowledge Augmentation in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the knowledge-confidence gaps in Large Language Models (LLMs) during knowledge augmentation to enhance knowledge capabilities and foster cognitive behaviors that better distinguish knowns from unknowns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a meta-cognitive framework that uses internal cognitive signals to partition the knowledge space into mastered, confused, and missing regions for targeted knowledge expansion, and introduces a cognitive consistency mechanism to align subjective certainty with objective accuracy, thereby enhancing knowledge capabilities and clarifying knowledge boundaries.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge augmentation is not merely a matter of acquiring more knowledge, but of knowing more clearly what they know and what they do not.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework (CGKE + CDKC) significantly outperforms strong baselines across diverse QA benchmarks.
Iterative evolution with two full 'expansion-calibration' cycles yields substantial additional performance gains.
The framework improves the correlation between internal confidence and accuracy, indicating enhanced meta-cognitive alignment.
Ablation studies show that resolving cognitive ambiguity (Knowledge Confused region) is more impactful for expanding knowledge boundaries than reinforcing mastered facts.
The framework demonstrates robustness across varying knowledge grounding states (weakly, partially, and well-grounded).
papers.abstract: Knowledge augmentation has significantly enhanced the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge-intensive tasks. However, existing methods typically operate on the simplistic premise that model performance equates with internal knowledge, overlooking the knowledge-confidence gaps that lead to overconfident errors or uncertain truths. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel meta-cognitive framework for reliable knowledge augmentation via differentiated intervention and alignment. Our approach leverages internal cognitive signals to partition the knowledge space into mastered, confused, and missing regions, guiding targeted knowledge expansion. Furthermore, we introduce a cognitive consistency mechanism to synchronize subjective certainty with objective accuracy, ensuring calibrated knowledge boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate the our framework consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating its rationality in not only enhancing knowledge capabilities but also fostering cognitive behaviors that better distinguish knowns from unknowns.

papers.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does truth in LLMs have a multi-dimensional representation (concept cone) rather than a single linear direction, and can such cones causally mediate truth-related behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that truth in LLMs is represented as a multi-dimensional cone in activation space, and that interventions using these cones can reliably steer model outputs on true/false propositions while preserving unrelated capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Multi-dimensional concept cones can reliably steer LLM behavior on true/false propositions across architectures and sizes, revealing a robust subspace of activation vectors that modulate factuality.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-related directions are localized in middle to later layers, with the final token position being most effective for interventions.
Multi-dimensional concept cones for truth exist and can causally mediate truthful behavior across different model families and sizes.
Increasing cone dimensionality generally improves steering effectiveness, but beyond a point, ASR declines, especially in smaller models.
The discovered truth directions are specific and do not significantly affect general instruction-following capabilities (low KL divergence on Alpaca).
The classic DIM direction aligns only with the first axis of the cone; other axes are orthogonal, indicating additional structure.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively small open-source models (1.5B–7B parameters) and may not generalize to larger frontier models.
The operationalization of truth is narrow, limited to simple unambiguous propositional facts, and does not capture more complex notions of truth.
The method does not guarantee discovery of a maximally informative or interpretable subspace, and individual cone axes lack semantic meaning.
future_direction: Pair cones with automated clustering or sparse autoencoding to assign semantic meaning to basis vectors.
Extend the method to larger, instruction-tuned models.
Extend to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational abilities but often generate falsehoods. Prior work suggests that the truthfulness of simple propositions can be represented as a single linear direction in a model's internal activations, but this may not fully capture its underlying geometry. In this work, we extend the concept cone framework, recently introduced for modeling refusal, to the domain of truth. We identify multi-dimensional cones that causally mediate truth-related behavior across multiple LLM families. Our results are supported by three lines of evidence: (i) causal interventions reliably flip model responses to factual statements, (ii) learned cones generalize across model architectures, and (iii) cone-based interventions preserve unrelated model behavior. These findings reveal the richer, multidirectional structure governing simple true/false propositions in LLMs and highlight concept cones as a promising tool for probing abstract behaviors.

papers.title: Task Schema and Binding: A Double Dissociation Study of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning decompose into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning decomposes into two separable mechanisms—Task Schema (encoded in late MLP layers) and Binding (encoded in the residual stream)—and demonstrates a Prior-Schema trade-off where schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning operates through a compositional mechanism with two separable components (Task Schema and Binding), and the bottleneck for binding failures is attentional (recency bias) rather than output-level prior competition.
papers.key_findings:
Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching, proving separable mechanisms.
Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman ρ=-0.596, p<0.001).
Architecture generality: The Task Schema mechanism operates across all tested Transformer families and the non-Transformer Mamba model.
Binding failures are primarily due to recency-biased mis-attention (72.7%) and not prior competition (0%).
Task Schema is encoded in late MLP layers (75-95% network depth) and is robust to demonstration ordering.
papers.limitation:
Model scale: only tested up to 13B parameters; 70B+ and proprietary models remain untested.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning are not tested.
Binding control is incomplete (62% success rate).
Prior measurement (zero-shot probability) is an imperfect proxy that may miss latent associations.
Ecological validity: controlled tasks may not fully represent real-world ICL with noisy demonstrations and ambiguous specifications.
future_direction: Testing larger models (70B+).
Investigating Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning.
Improving binding control (e.g., via attention weight patching or activation steering).
papers.abstract: We provide causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning (ICL) decomposes into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations). Through activation patching experiments across 9 models from 7 Transformer families plus Mamba (370M-13B parameters), we establish three key findings: 1. Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching -- proving separable mechanisms 2. Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman rho = -0.596, p < 0.001, N=28 task-model pairs) 3. Architecture generality: The mechanism operates across all tested architectures including the non-Transformer Mamba These findings offer a mechanistic account of the ICL puzzle that contrasts with prior views treating ICL as a monolithic mechanism (whether retrieval-based, gradient descent-like, or purely Bayesian). By establishing that Schema and Binding are neurally dissociable -- not merely behavioral modes -- we provide causal evidence for dual-process theories of ICL. Models rely on Task Schema when prior knowledge is absent, but prior knowledge interferes through attentional mis-routing (72.7% recency bias) rather than direct output competition (0%). This explains why arbitrary mappings succeed (zero prior leads to full Schema reliance) while factual overrides fail -- and reveals that the true bottleneck is attentional, not output-level. Practical implications: Understanding these dual mechanisms enables more efficient prompt engineering -- reliable schema transfer reduces required demonstrations for novel tasks, while prior-aware design can mitigate the 38% binding failure rate in high-prior scenarios, improving ICL system reliability in production deployments.

papers.title: Optimal ablation for interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we better quantify the importance of model components for interpretability by using an ablation method that minimizes expected loss?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces optimal ablation (OA), a method for ablating model components by setting them to a constant that minimizes expected loss, leading to better component importance estimates and improved performance in circuit discovery, factual recall localization, and latent prediction.
papers.conclusion: Optimal ablation is a theoretically and empirically better method for ablating model components, improving component importance quantification and downstream interpretability tasks.
papers.key_findings:
OA provides a theoretically grounded way to measure component importance by minimizing spoofing effects.
OA yields lower ablation loss gaps compared to prior methods like zero, mean, resample, and counterfactual ablation.
OA improves circuit discovery, producing smaller and lower-loss circuits.
OA improves causal tracing for factual recall, providing more precise localization.
OA improves latent prediction via OCA lens, achieving better predictive power and causal faithfulness.
papers.limitation: OA requires optimizing constants for each component and subtask, which can be computationally expensive.
future_direction: More efficient optimization methods for OA constants
Scaling interpretability techniques to larger models
papers.abstract: Interpretability studies often involve tracing the flow of information through machine learning models to identify specific model components that perform relevant computations for tasks of interest. Prior work quantifies the importance of a model component on a particular task by measuring the impact of performing ablation on that component, or simulating model inference with the component disabled. We propose a new method, optimal ablation (OA), and show that OA-based component importance has theoretical and empirical advantages over measuring importance via other ablation methods. We also show that OA-based component importance can benefit several downstream interpretability tasks, including circuit discovery, localization of factual recall, and latent prediction.

papers.title: CoME: An Unlearning-based Approach to Conflict-free Model Editing
papers.research_question: How to mitigate knowledge conflicts in model editing for LLMs by selectively removing outdated knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: CoME is a framework that enhances model editing accuracy by unlearning outdated knowledge during the integration of new information, reducing knowledge conflicts.
papers.conclusion: CoME effectively mitigates knowledge conflicts in LLMs by unlearning outdated knowledge during editing, improving reliability and consistency.
papers.key_findings:
CoME improves editing accuracy (Efficacy and Generality) on GPT-J and LLaMA-3.
It reduces interference from outdated knowledge, leading to more reliable responses.
Locality is slightly affected but balanced by restricting unlearning parameters.
CoME is robust as the number of edits increases.
Ablation studies show that removing outdated knowledge and restricting parameters are crucial.
papers.limitation:
The unlearning process requires additional computational resources.
CoME may not be suitable for temporal knowledge where older information is still useful.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often retain outdated or incorrect information from pre-training, which undermines their reliability. While model editing methods have been developed to address such errors without full re-training, they frequently suffer from knowledge conflicts, where outdated information interferes with new knowledge. In this work, we propose Conflict-free Model Editing (CoME), a novel framework that enhances the accuracy of knowledge updates in LLMs by selectively removing outdated knowledge. CoME leverages unlearning to mitigate knowledge interference, allowing new information to be integrated without compromising relevant linguistic features. Through experiments on GPT-J and LLaMA-3 using Counterfact and ZsRE datasets, we demonstrate that CoME improves both editing accuracy and model reliability when applied to existing editing methods. Our results highlight that the targeted removal of outdated knowledge is crucial for enhancing model editing effectiveness and maintaining the model's generative performance.

papers.title: Editing Factual Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces KNOWLEDGE EDITOR, a hyper-network-based method to edit factual knowledge in language models efficiently and reliably without retraining or fine-tuning, while preserving other knowledge and ensuring consistency across paraphrases.
papers.conclusion: KNOWLEDGE EDITOR provides an effective and reliable method for editing factual knowledge in language models, meeting desiderata of generality, reliability, and consistency.
papers.key_findings:
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR achieves high success rate and retain accuracy on fact-checking and question answering tasks.
Using paraphrase supervision during training improves consistency across semantically equivalent inputs.
The updates predicted by KNOWLEDGE EDITOR are sparse and concentrated on attention weight matrices in lower layers, contrasting with gradient-based methods.
KNOWLEDGE EDITOR outperforms fine-tuning and constrained fine-tuning baselines in terms of retaining previous knowledge and generalization to paraphrases.
The hyper-network learns to project gradients to a different direction that preserves other knowledge while editing the target fact.
future_direction: Exploring multiple updates in a loop for editing.
Investigating the mechanism of knowledge encoding in LMs through the lens of editing.
papers.abstract: The factual knowledge acquired during pretraining and stored in the parameters of Language Models (LMs) can be useful in downstream tasks (e.g., question answering or textual inference). However, some facts can be incorrectly induced or become obsolete over time. We present KNOWLEDGEEDITOR, a method which can be used to edit this knowledge and, thus, fix 'bugs' or unexpected predictions without the need for expensive retraining or fine-tuning. Besides being computationally efficient, KNOWLEDGEEDITOR does not require any modifications in LM pretraining (e.g., the use of meta-learning). In our approach, we train a hyper-network with constrained optimization to modify a fact without affecting the rest of the knowledge; the trained hyper-network is then used to predict the weight update at test time. We show KNOWL-EDGEEDITOR's efficacy with two popular architectures and knowledge-intensive tasks: i) a BERT model fine-tuned for fact-checking, and ii) a sequence-to-sequence BART model for question answering. With our method, changing a prediction on the specific wording of a query tends to result in a consistent change in predictions also for its paraphrases. We show that this can be further encouraged by exploiting (e.g., automatically-generated) paraphrases during training. Interestingly, our hyper-network can be regarded as a 'probe' revealing which components need to be changed to manipulate factual knowledge; our analysis shows that the updates tend to be concentrated on a small subset of components. 1 How is Namibia's capital city called? papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Hallucinate Less by Thinking More: Aspect-Based Causal Abstention for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we enable early abstention in Large Language Models by analyzing the internal diversity of their parametric knowledge through causal inference to prevent unreliable responses?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Aspect-Based Causal Abstention (ABCA), a framework that enables early abstention in LLMs by modeling knowledge heterogeneity through aspect-conditioned causal inference, improving abstention reliability and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: ABCA provides a causally principled framework for early abstention by probing diverse knowledge aspects, effectively reducing hallucinations and offering interpretable abstention decisions.
papers.key_findings:
ABCA achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple abstention benchmarks, outperforming existing post-hoc methods.
The framework distinguishes between knowledge conflict (Type-1) and knowledge insufficiency (Type-2) abstention, providing interpretable decisions.
ABCA improves answering accuracy on answerable questions while maintaining high abstention accuracy on unanswerable ones.
The dual-agent aspect discovery mechanism effectively identifies causally valid conditioning variables and aspects.
Case studies reveal limitations such as invalid aspect conditioning leading to incorrect abstention and aggregation on spurious facts despite consensus.
papers.limitation:
Invalid aspect conditioning (e.g., using a non-meaningful dimension like 'Number of') can lead to incorrect abstention decisions.
Strong agreement across discovered aspects may still lead to incorrect answers if the aspects overlook disambiguating information in the query.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often produce fluent but factually incorrect responses, a phenomenon known as hallucination. Abstention, where the model chooses not to answer and instead outputs phrases such as "I don't know", is a common safeguard. However, existing abstention methods typically rely on post-generation signals, such as generation variations or feedback, which limits their ability to prevent unreliable responses in advance. In this paper, we introduce Aspect-Based Causal Abstention (ABCA), a new framework that enables early abstention by analysing the internal diversity of LLM knowledge through causal inference. This diversity reflects the multifaceted nature of parametric knowledge acquired from various sources, representing diverse aspects such as disciplines, legal contexts, or temporal frames. ABCA estimates causal effects conditioned on these aspects to assess the reliability of knowledge relevant to a given query. Based on these estimates, we enable two types of abstention: Type-1, where aspect effects are inconsistent (knowledge conflict), and Type-2, where aspect effects consistently support abstention (knowledge insufficiency). Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that ABCA improves abstention reliability, achieves state-of-the-art performance, and enhances the interpretability of abstention decisions.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: The Rise of Parameter Specialization for Knowledge Storage in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the way knowledge is stored in MLP parameters and the performance of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Stronger large language models exhibit higher parameter specialization for knowledge storage in MLPs, and this specialization improves the efficiency of knowledge utilization and reduces hallucination.
papers.conclusion: Enhanced parameter specialization for knowledge storage correlates with superior performance in LLMs, and optimizing this specialization improves task performance and reduces hallucination, highlighting the importance of aligning knowledge storage with retrieval mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger models show higher parameter specialization, with PSS correlating strongly with performance on knowledge tasks.
Parameter specialization increases with model scale within the same family.
Parameter specialization evolves during pretraining, increasing in later training steps.
Fine-tuning that enhances parameter specialization (FT-PV) improves performance on knowledge tasks and reduces hallucination compared to other fine-tuning strategies.
Specialized knowledge distribution helps compress knowledge and reduce interference from irrelevant information.
papers.limitation:
Only examined knowledge parameter specialization within the MLP, not attention modules.
Tested models only up to 14B parameters due to GPU limitations.
future_direction: Progressively narrow the focus to individual neurons to measure more precise Parameter Specialization.
Extend the concept to other model architectures like Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs).
papers.abstract: Over time, a growing wave of large language models from various series has been introduced to the community. Researchers are striving to maximize the performance of language models with constrained parameter sizes. However, from a microscopic perspective, there has been limited research on how to better store knowledge in model parameters, particularly within MLPs, to enable more effective utilization of this knowledge by the model. In this work, we analyze twenty publicly available open-source large language models to investigate the relationship between their strong performance and the way knowledge is stored in their corresponding MLP parameters. Our findings reveal that as language models become more advanced and demonstrate stronger knowledge capabilities, their parameters exhibit increased specialization. Specifically, parameters in the MLPs tend to be more focused on encoding similar types of knowledge. We experimentally validate that this specialized distribution of knowledge contributes to improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in these models. Furthermore, by conducting causal training experiments, we confirm that this specialized knowledge distribution plays a critical role in improving the model's efficiency in leveraging stored knowledge.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Drift in Large Language Models: An Examination of Adaptive Retention Across Sequential Inputs
papers.research_question: How does Contextual Feature Drift (CFD) manifest in LLMs, and what factors (input length, semantic similarity, entropy, temporal intervals) influence it?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces and investigates Contextual Feature Drift (CFD), a phenomenon where context retention in LLMs decays over sequential inputs, and shows that extended input lengths, lower semantic similarity, and high-entropy sequences exacerbate CFD.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that CFD is a significant phenomenon in LLMs, influenced by input length, semantic similarity, temporal gaps, and entropy, and addressing it is crucial for applications requiring consistent context retention.
papers.key_findings:
Extended input lengths lead to decreased context retention, with cosine similarity dropping from 0.92 at 100 tokens to 0.73 at 500 tokens.
Lower semantic similarity between consecutive inputs leads to more pronounced drift, with similarity scores dropping to 0.65 for high topic drift.
Longer temporal intervals between inputs cause greater drift, with cosine similarity dropping from 0.89 at 5 seconds to 0.61 at 30 seconds.
Higher entropy inputs reduce context stability, with stability scores declining from 0.91 for low entropy to 0.67 for high entropy.
Positional encoding stability decreases with longer sequences, from 0.93 at 50 tokens to 0.66 at 500 tokens.
papers.limitation:
Model selection confined to a single open-source LLM architecture limits generalizability across different model structures.
Experimental conditions constrained by synthetic input generation lack the variability inherent to natural language environments.
future_direction: Cross-model CFD comparisons to evaluate whether drift patterns are consistent across architectures.
Expanding experimental setups to include more diverse linguistic datasets to better mirror authentic conversational data.
Developing more granular CFD metrics to capture subtle drift variations, such as at the layer-wise or attention-head level.
papers.abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence have led to models capable of generating highly coherent language, yet limitations in retaining contextual alignment across extended inputs remain challenging. Contextual Feature Drift (CFD) emerges as a significant yet underexplored phenomenon, describing how sequential input dynamics affect contextual consistency within model outputs. This paper investigates CFD within an open-source transformer-based model, employing controlled synthetic data sequences to analyze context retention as influenced by factors such as input length, semantic similarity, entropy variability, and temporal intervals. Experimental results reveal that extended input lengths, lower semantic similarity, and high-entropy sequences exacerbate CFD, demonstrating quantifiable declines in context retention. Positional encoding and attention allocation metrics provide further insight into feature drift, showing potential vulnerabilities for applications relying on consistent sequential context, including conversational AI and recommendation systems. The study highlights the criticality of mitigating CFD for enhancing model reliability, positing that strategic adjustments to LLM architectures and training methods may support more robust applications requiring sustained context fidelity. Through this investigation, the findings contribute a foundational understanding of CFD, establishing its relevance for future research and LLM development.

papers.title: Pathological Truth Bias in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the extent and mechanistic cause of pathological truth bias—the tendency of vision-language models to agree with patently false, visually absurd statements—in instruction-tuned generative VLMs compared to contrastive encoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MATS framework to audit pathological truth bias in VLMs and uses activation patching to causally localize the bias to mid-to-late cross-attention layers in generative models and pooled/projection components in contrastive encoders.
papers.conclusion: Pathological truth bias is a systemic issue in instruction-tuned VLMs, and combining behavioral audits (MATS) with causal interventions (activation patching) identifies concrete repair targets in cross-attention and projection components.
papers.key_findings:
Instruction-tuned generative VLMs (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen-VL-chat) show catastrophically low Spatial Consistency Scores (SCS≈1–3%) and high Incorrect Agreement Rates (IAR≈75–80%).
Contrastive encoders (CLIP, SigLIP) are substantially more robust, with SCS≈57–68% and IAR≈8–12%.
Activation patching successfully restores correct outputs in 23% of cases for LLaVA, with the largest causal effects concentrated in mid-to-late cross-attention layers.
For CLIP, patching pooled/projection components yields significant representational shifts (mean ∆ cos≈0.05–0.07).
The bias is linked to instruction-tuning practices that favor agreeableness over truthfulness, extending sycophancy observations to the multimodal domain.
papers.limitation:
Dataset scope is narrow, focusing only on color, object presence, and spatial predicates; results may differ for temporal, causal, or more abstract relations.
Strict TRUE/FALSE parsing and forced binary framing may bias outcomes relative to open-ended prompts or richer response formats.
Patch success is partial and donor-dependent, with the best loci repairing only a minority of examples.
Evaluation is limited to specific public checkpoints and prompt templates; newer models or different instruction-tuning recipes may alter the observed profiles.
future_direction: Mitigation experiments: surgical edits (head-level fine-tuning), projection calibration, and run-time verifiers.
Large-scale replication and generalization across more checkpoints, architectures, and alignment recipes.
Causal chain-of-effect mapping to track activation flows through subsequent layers after successful transplants.
papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are improving quickly, but standard benchmarks can hide systematic failures that reduce real world trust. We introduce MATS (Multimodal Audit for Truthful Spatialization), a compact behavioral audit that measures whether models reject visually contradicted statements, and two metrics Spatial Consistency Score (SCS) and Incorrect Agreement Rate (IAR). Instruction tuned generative VLMs (LLaVA 1.5, QwenVLchat) exhibit very low SCS and high IAR, while contrastive encoders (CLIP, SigLIP) are far more robust. Activation patching causally localizes failure loci (mid to late cross attention for generative models, pooled projection components for contrastive models) and suggests concrete repair paths.

papers.title: Hopping Too Late: Exploring the Limitations of Large Language Models on Multi-Hop Queries
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally compute answers to multi-hop queries, and why do they sometimes fail?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a sequential latent reasoning pathway in LLMs for two-hop queries and introduces a novel 'back-patching' analysis method that can correct many previously incorrect answers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs use a sequential pathway for latent multi-hop reasoning, and the introduced back-patching method can improve performance, opening opportunities for understanding and improving such reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The bridge entity (first hop answer) is resolved in the early layers of the model.
The second hop is resolved in later layers, only after the first hop is resolved.
The sequential nature can cause failure if the later layers lack the necessary knowledge or functionality.
Back-patching (patching a later hidden representation back to an earlier layer) can correct up to 66% of previously incorrect cases.
Information about the bridge entity propagates from the first hop position to the last token position, primarily through middle layers.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic methods used (e.g., Patchscopes, vocabulary projections) are approximations.
The study focuses on one prominent latent reasoning pathway, but others likely exist.
The work examines only two-hop queries, not more complex multi-step reasoning.
Back-patching is not a practical inference method without an efficient way to select source and target layers a priori.
future_direction: Expanding the analysis to queries with three or more hops and additional reasoning tasks.
Developing methods to efficiently select source and target layers for back-patching to make it a viable inference method.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can solve complex multi-step problems, but little is known about how these computations are implemented internally. Motivated by this, we study how LLMs answer multi-hop queries such as "The spouse of the performer of Imagine is". These queries require two information extraction steps: a latent one for resolving the first hop ("the performer of Imagine") into the bridge entity (John Lennon), and another for resolving the second hop ("the spouse of John Lennon") into the target entity (Yoko Ono). Understanding how the latent step is computed internally is key to understanding the overall computation. By carefully analyzing the internal computations of transformer-based LLMs, we discover that the bridge entity is resolved in the early layers of the model. Then, only after this resolution, the two-hop query is solved in the later layers. Because the second hop commences in later layers, there could be cases where these layers no longer encode the necessary knowledge for correctly predicting the answer. Motivated by this, we propose a novel "back-patching" analysis method whereby a hidden representation from a later layer is patched back to an earlier layer. We find that in up to 66% of previously incorrect cases there exists a back-patch that results in the correct generation of the answer, showing that the later layers indeed sometimes lack the needed functionality. Overall, our methods and findings open further opportunities for understanding and improving latent reasoning in transformer-based LLMs.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
papers.research_question: Do deeper language models use their depth to compose more features for higher-order computations, or do they merely spread the same kinds of computation out over more layers?
papers.core_contribution: Deeper language models do not use their increased depth to learn new kinds of computation; instead, they spread the same computation over more layers and use the second half primarily for fine-grained refinement of the output probability distribution.
papers.conclusion: Current large language models underutilize the second half of their layers, which may explain why increasing depth leads to diminishing returns in performance for stacked Transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in the second half of the model contribute much less to the residual stream than those in the first half, with a clear phase transition around the middle.
Skipping layers in the second half has a much smaller effect on future computations and output predictions compared to skipping layers in the first half.
For multi-hop tasks, there is no evidence that models use increased depth to compose sub-results; later computation steps do not use more layers.
Linear maps from a shallow model's residual stream to a deeper model's show a diagonal pattern, indicating the deeper model 'stretches out' the same computation rather than performing novel computation.
The second half of the network is devoted to refining the current token's probability distribution, not computing reusable sub-results for future tokens.
papers.limitation:
The findings are a case study on Llama and Qwen models and may not hold for other model types.
The work does not answer how models solve problems without depth dependence.
The linear map analysis in Section 3.4 relies on a single model pair due to resource constraints.
The exploration in Section 3.5 relies on manual study of individual trained models.
future_direction: Develop an automatic metric to measure the correspondence of computation to the parse tree.
Verify the findings with more resources on different and deeper models.
Investigate how models solve problems without depth dependence.
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs are increasingly deep, and depth correlates with performance, albeit with diminishing returns. However, do these models use their depth efficiently? Do they compose more features to create higher-order computations that are impossible in shallow models, or do they merely spread the same kinds of computation out over more layers? To address these questions, we analyze the residual stream of the Llama 3.1, Qwen 3, and OLMo 2 family of models. We find: First, comparing the output of the sublayers to the residual stream reveals that layers in the second half contribute much less than those in the first half, with a clear phase transition between the two halves. Second, skipping layers in the second half has a much smaller effect on future computations and output predictions. Third, for multihop tasks, we are unable to find evidence that models are using increased depth to compose subresults in examples involving many hops. Fourth, we seek to directly address whether deeper models are using their additional layers to perform new kinds of computation. To do this, we train linear maps from the residual stream of a shallow model to a deeper one. We find that layers with the same relative depth map best to each other, suggesting that the larger model simply spreads the same computations out over its many layers. All this evidence suggests that deeper models are not using their depth to learn new kinds of computation, but only using the greater depth to perform more fine-grained adjustments to the residual. This may help explain why increasing scale leads to diminishing returns for stacked Transformer architectures.

papers.title: Testing Pre-trained Language Models’ Understanding of Distributivity via Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: To what extent do pre-trained language models grasp semantic knowledge regarding the phenomenon of distributivity?
